To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability of adult female conspecifics to modulate HPA responses to novelty in guinea pigs is not dependent on the presence of maternal nurturant behavior or on the presence of the offspring's mother, but rather emerges during the peri-adolescent period and is likely to facilitate the redirection of offspring behavior to unrelated adult conspecifics.

(1) the ability of unfamiliar females to moderate HPA activity emerges during the peri-adolescent period; (2) this ability is not dependent on nurturing behavior by the unfamiliar female, and (3) the ability of the mother to moderate HPA and sexual responses of her offspring appears to be specific to the mother-offspring dyad.

the ability of an unfamiliar adult female to modulate hypothalamic-puitary-adrenal function in periadolescent offspring fully emerges during the second postnatal month in guinea pigs, and that the mother inhibits the development of sexual behavior and plasma androgen levels in her sons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of social behavior and its relationship with endocrine and autonomic activity in guinea pigs, and has focused on two major issues.
the development of the neuroendocrine mechanisms that underlie the expression of social behavior, and how these mechanisms are modified by social experiences.

the ontogeny of social influences on the neuroendocrine stress response, the ontogeny and consequences of the mother's ability to moderate this stress response and the consequences of this ability for the redirection of social behaviors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the periadolescents are more responsive to their mother, but that the unfamiliar female is more likely to be a sexual stimulus.
the presence of an adult female, whether mother or unfamiliar, reduces the HPA response of the offspring to novelty.
the presence of either a mother or unfamiliar adult females during novelty exposure in the periadolescence is beneficial for the guinea pig offspring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of a female in the periadolescence period has profound effects on both HPA and reproductive function.

the ability of the mother to regulate the behavioral and neuroendocrine responses of her offspring emerges during the periadolscent period, and that the mother's ability to moderate the responses of her offspring is not due to nurturance, but rather is a result of the mother's ability as a social partner.

the presence of either the biological mother or an unrelated female can moderate the hypothalamic-puitary-adrenal response to stress in periadolescent male guinea pigs, but the behavioral and physiological consequences of these responses are different.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the presence of the biological mother during a novel experience reduces the stress responses and the presence of an unfamiliar adult female has no effect on stress responses but has a profound effect on the behavioral responses of peri-adolescent guineapigs.
periadolescent offspring are not simply miniature adults.
the ability to moderate the stress response emerges in the second postnatal month in the guinea pig.
